item.title: We Need a New Language, a New Imagination, a New Story... and It Won't Come from AI
item.description: Adapted from a public lecture given for Regis University’s Ignatian Mission Day, the essay wrestles with the crisis of communication across political divides, the attacks on universities across the country linked to Project 2025, and the emergence of Artificial Intelligence as a powerful new challenge in the landscape of Jesuit higher education. Identifying the root illness of our times as a diseased and captive cultural imagination, the author calls for responses that heal and break open the imagination. The poets and prophets, artists and storytellers, share common cause with the Ignatian imagination – a contemplative, transcendent horizon, grounded in the concrete real – that is the lodestar for our work across all the university disciplines.

item.title: Generative AI and the Ignatian Pedagogical Paradigm
item.description: A group of seven faculty members, the Digital Teaching Fellows (DTF), were formed in 2023 to explore issues related to generative AI at a Jesuit university in the United States. The group incorporated generative AI assignments into their courses and conducted a survey assessing students’ experiences with generative AI in the course. Drawing from both quantitative and qualitative analysis, the DTF reached two key conclusions. First, despite their reservations, students’ overall receptiveness to generative AI integration creates a fitting moment for thoughtful pedagogical innovation. Second, our findings reveal a critical gap between generative AI’s current implementation and its potential to support higher-level learning goals. To address the two findings, the DTF propose a systematic, Ignatian pedagogy-driven approach to generative AI integration.

item.title: The Current State of Global Engagement within U.S. Jesuit Institutions: Challenges and Opportunities
item.description: Jesuit education aims to cultivate global citizens who actively engage with the world and champion social justice. As economic and social ties grow increasingly interconnected, Jesuit institutions need to develop innovative international learning opportunities for students. In this study, using publicly available IIE Open Doors data from the past two decades, we assess international student enrollment and study abroad initiatives at U.S. Jesuit institutions and compare these metrics against national trends. The results suggest that U.S. Jesuit institutions have substantial potential to invest in and reap the benefits of global engagement. Grounded in the Jesuit mission and the Inspirational Paradigm for Jesuit Business Education, we analyze key factors that hinder and support Jesuit institutions in advancing their global engagement efforts. This study provides statistical insights into the current state of global engagement within U.S. Jesuit institutions and offers transferable examples on promoting Jesuit education on the global stage.

item.title: Academic Integrity, Generative Software, and Catholic, Jesuit Higher Education in the Context of Neoliberal Global Society
item.description: This is a reflection on different aspects of higher education and generative software (so-called 'ai') in light of Ignatian discernment, especially the key consideration of "context." Drawing on administrative and classroom work at a Jesuit university in the United States, Catholic Social Teaching principles, papal teaching on social justice and technology, and an honest consideration of generative software's social, corporate, and ecological contexts, this reflection soberly assesses the fraught nature of complicity with such neoliberal, exploitative, and extractive contexts for Jesuit institutions of higher education. While it is easier to go along with mainstream economic and cultural assumptions, I claim here that the problems with generative software systems and the practices of the companies that make them available are so antithetical to the stated aims of Jesuit education and Catholic Social Teaching that debates about the functionality of generative software in educational spaces are posterior to the debates that matter most.

item.title: “Cool People Doing Good Work”: A Rights-Based, Relational Model for Research, Teaching, and Outreach Rooted in Urban Settings
item.description: Urban Catholic institutions of higher education are being challenged to do more when it comes to working with communities that surround them at the same time as they face multiple external pressure and must clearly define the value of their mission. In this article, we present a model for community-engaged practices that emerge from the ground up to move these institutions more in line with Catholic Social Teaching. “Cool People Doing Good Work” is an adaptable model centered around relationship building and authentic engagement with local experts, stakeholders, and community members that then builds to institutional change. This model places integral humanism at the forefront. This humanism, sponsored by the Church, emphasizes the development of human dignity over that of the market. The model developed is countercultural in that it approaches the development of the person and community, while centering subsidiarity. We first root the model in Catholic mission and values, then describe its steps. We end with an example of its application in a midwestern city. This article seeks to highlight the ways in which community-engaged work pushes urban institutions to adopt and recognize the work by incorporating it into their broader mission.

item.title: Beyond the Prompt: Coding the Magis in the Age of AI
item.description: As a scholar-practitioner in Jesuit higher education, I’ve witnessed how generative AI is not merely a tool students use—it’s a formative force that shapes how they reflect, imagine, and even pray. Drawing on the Catholic imagination, Ignatian pedagogy, and sociological frameworks like liquid modernity, I argue that Jesuit institutions must respond not just technologically and reactively, but actively anticipate methods of integrating AI both theologically and pedagogically. I introduce the concept of Imaginative Intelligence as a formative goal—an embodied, sacramental way of knowing that invites depth, wonder, and resistance to automation. This is not a call to reject AI, but to reclaim the mission: to form students who are not just capable of generating responses, but of asking better questions. Who they become cannot be prompted. It must be practiced, accompanied, and formed in freedom. This, I suggest, is the best way to advance Catholic and Jesuit identity for higher education in today's context.

item.title: The popemobile race: How car companies rallied to serve a papal passenger
item.description:
VATICAN CITY (CNS) -- From horse-drawn ornate wooden carriages to a bulletproof all-electric vehicle, the papal modes of transport have evolved to keep the pope safe, seen and saving the planet.

The first time a car was offered to a pope was after the 1903 election of St. Pius X when the Archdiocese of New York donated one, said Sandro Barbagallo, curator of historical collections at the Vatican Museums.

"But the pope refused it," he told reporters at a new exhibit featuring select popemobiles Oct. 28.

The pope politely declined the gift, he said, in part because a car was useless at the time since a dispute with the Italian government over the sovereignty of the Holy See kept popes confined to Vatican City from 1870 to 1929, and because he preferred walking in the Vatican Gardens and hearing "the sound of horses' hooves along the path rather than the sound of an internal combustion engine."

However, the pope's limited opportunities to travel didn't stop other eager Catholics from wanting to share this new invention; an association of Catholic women in Milan gave Pope Pius XI, who was elected in 1922, a car made by the Italian manufacturer Bianchi, which was expanding from making bicycles and motorcycles to automobiles.

Why manufacturers were eager to supply cars for the pope

When the 1929 Lateran Pacts finally allowed popes to go freely outside Vatican City walls, many car manufacturers started competing to give the pope a car, Barbagallo said, "so they could boast the title of supplier to the papal household." 

The first car that arrived immediately after the signing of the Lateran Pacts was a U.S. Graham-Paige 837, he said. Pope Pius XI ventured out in it -- becoming the first pope to put the rubber to the road -- to St. John Lateran to celebrate Mass to mark the 50th anniversary of his ordination.

Shortly thereafter, a Citroën and a Mercedes-Benz arrived, Barbagallo said, "but the Mercedes was already a cut above" all the others because it had been "specifically tailored for the pope."

For example, he said, the Graham-Paige was just a standard model whose backseat had been replaced with a single seat. And even though it is an elegant, beautiful vehicle, "it looks more like a gangster's car when you see it."

Instead, the Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 limousine given to Pope Pius XI in 1930 has a large silk-brocade upholstered chair for the pope that faces other seats for his assistants in the back, and it has buttons for the pope to push that light up a dial in the driver's section indicating "go faster," "go slower," turn right," "turn left," "stop" and "go home." 

"Those were the electronics in 1930," said Marcus Breitschwerdt, the CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage, during a news conference at the museums Oct. 28, unveiling the new, temporary exhibit of vehicles specifically designed and donated by the German company to the popes. 

This fine-tuned attention to the unique needs and ministry of a papal passenger helped solidify an almost 100-year relationship between the Vatican and Mercedes-Benz, which was also celebrating the 140th anniversary of Karl Benz submitting a patent for his gas-powered vehicle in 1886, launching the invention of the automobile.

From papal transport to the 'popemobile'

Another "invention" would eventually be made in the 20th century: the iconic popemobile, that is, a vehicle that could not only get a pope from place to place like with his special limos and sedans, but also let him be more visible and close to the people.

Back in the old days, the pope was hoisted up high in a grand "sedia gestatoria," or portable papal throne, carried on the shoulders of 12 "sediari" or chair-carriers to move the pope through the crowds of the faithful during special ceremonies.

The first to create a vehicular version of that was Toyota, which modified an all-white 1975 Land Cruiser by removing the roof and rear body panel so the car was open and St. Paul VI could stand and offer his blessings.

However, there was nothing to sit on, Barbagallo said. So, for St. John Paul II, somebody retrofitted a white swivel seat taken from "a barber's chair -- I think it belonged to John XXIII – that they had to place on a metal base." 

Next came the all-white open-air 1980 Fiat Campagnola jeep, whose use became short-lived after a gunman in the crowd shot at and hit St. John Paul in 1981, after which all vehicles had to be made bulletproof.

An electric popemobile and a message of encounter

The popemobile continued to evolve in other ways to adapt to the times and the pope's agenda of greater sustainability, with the first fully electric, emissions-free popemobile created by Mercedes-Benz for Pope Francis before the 2025 Holy Year and used by Pope Leo XIV during his 2026 trip in France.

When greeting delegates from Mercedes-Benz at the Vatican Oct. 28, Pope Leo said, "Over the decades, the popemobile has evolved from a means of transportation into an instrument of encounter, enabling the pontiff to draw closer to the faithful during pastoral visits and public celebrations."

"In this way, your work has helped facilitate the Church's mission of reaching out to people and bringing a message of faith, hope and charity to the world," he said, encouraging them to continue "placing technological innovation at the service of human dignity, care for creation and the common good."

item.title: USCCB Statement on Pope Leo XIV Voting in Midterm Elections in USA
item.description:
WASHINGTON – Earlier today, the Holy See Press Office announced that Pope Leo XIV had voted in the 2026 midterm elections with a mail-in ballot. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) has offered the following statement from its spokesperson, Chieko Noguchi, executive director of public affairs:

“As Catholics and Americans, we are blessed to be able to participate in our nation’s political and public life. With the midterm elections approaching in the United States, the Conference has been encouraging Catholics to exercise their right to vote and to do so in a way that places our faith before our politics. In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility. The U.S. bishops have emphasized that it is not “who” one is voting for, but rather on encouraging Catholics to inform their conscience as they prepare to vote and to uphold human dignity and the common good in doing so.”

Learn more about Faith Before Politics: https://www.usccb.org/faithbeforepolitics

Videos* may be viewed here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLOxtm6LARtEo

*News outlets may share these videos and use screengrabs with attribution to the “U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops” (or “USCCB”)

item.title: Pope Leo urges ban on lethal autonomous weapons, stronger AI oversight
item.description:
VATICAN CITY (CNS) -- Pope Leo XIV called on world leaders to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons, warning that decisions affecting human life and freedom must never be left to artificial intelligence.

"Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight," the pope told  scientific experts and Vatican representatives during an audience at the Vatican Oct 30. 

The experts were in Rome taking part in a meeting -- organized by the Pontifical Academy for Life and the nonprofit Future of Life Institute -- to discuss the future of AI, its development and application.Artificial intelligence must be "disarmed," Pope Leo said, encouraging leaders meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons, because the future of artificial intelligence is "not pre-determined."

"As a technology developed by human beings, its future depends on the choices we make," he said.

The Vatican has repeatedly spoken out against AI weapons, including during the papal trip to France, where the pope warned against losing humanity amid what he called a “paradise of machines” and said ethical discernment is indispensable if technological progress is to promote integral human development.

Recalling Pope Francis' 2024 address to G7 leaders, in which his predecessor described artificial intelligence as both an "exciting and fearsome tool," Pope Leo reaffirmed in his Oct. 30 address that no machine should be entrusted with deciding whether to take a human life.

The pope's remarks were part of a broader appeal for stronger international institutions capable of translating ethical principles governing artificial intelligence into enforceable standards.

"We already know many of the ethical principles that should guide the development of artificial intelligence," he said. "What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice."

Such institutions, he said, must establish shared standards, independent oversight and clear accountability mechanisms that allow decisions involving AI to be examined and challenged, with appropriate remedies available when harm occurs.

Reflecting on his encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas," Pope Leo outlined considerations for the development and regulation of artificial intelligence, emphasizing that the direction of technological progress remains a matter of human choice.

Rather than treating AI development as a technological competition, he urged developers and policymakers to consider whom such systems serve and who risks being left behind.

"A reliable system that serves the human person is of greater value than one that is exceptionally powerful but whose consequences cannot be adequately foreseen or controlled," he said.

The pope also cautioned against proposals to grant AI systems rights or legal personhood, arguing that machines cannot be equated with human beings.

"Machines are tools, not persons," he said.

Granting artificial intelligence legal personhood, he warned, risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving people harmed by such systems without clear avenues for accountability.

"So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean," he said, quoting his encyclical. 

The pope also reiterated his belief that the benefits of technological development must be shared equitably, rather than concentrated in the hands of a few.

"Justice requires access to the benefits of innovation, including care, knowledge, tools and opportunities," he said, quoting his encyclical.

He ended by saying that what perhaps is most urgent is finding institutions capable of placing ethical guardrails into practice to "safeguard the global common good."
